opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core intuition comes from thinking about what structure in the data actually matters. When you predict raw pixels or tokens, you're forcing the model to account for every detail of the signal, including a huge amount of variability that is essentially irrelevant to the task. Think of an image: the exact texture of the grass, the precise noise in the lighting. A pixel-level objective spends capacity and, crucially, samples trying to model all of that.

In our work, we've been trying to understand learning on hierarchical data, models where the data is generated by composing features at different scales, a bit like a grammar. One thing that comes out clearly is that what makes learning possible with a reasonable number of samples is the ability to build invariances: to realize that different low-level configurations are, in a sense, synonyms, that they correspond to the same higher-level feature. Once you've grouped those together, the effective dimension of the problem collapses and you need far fewer examples to learn what comes next in the hierarchy.

Now, if your objective is in the latent space, you're directly rewarding the model for finding those representations that discard the irrelevant variability. You're predicting the "meaning," if you like, rather than the surface form. Whereas with token or pixel prediction, the invariances have to emerge somewhat indirectly. They can emerge, and in fact we see that next-token prediction does learn hierarchical structure progressively as the training set grows, but the signal you're using is diluted by all the details you're asked to reconstruct.

That said, I'd be careful about making it sound too clean. Latent prediction has its own difficulties: collapse, for instance, where the representation becomes trivial, and you need tricks to avoid that. And for language, tokens are already quite a compressed, meaningful representation, so the gap may be smaller than for vision. My guess is that the benefit is largest precisely where the raw signal is very high-dimensional and full of nuisance variability, which is why it has been so attractive for images and video.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it comes down to what you're forced to model. If you predict pixels, or tokens, you are asking the network to account for every bit of variance in the data, and most of that variance is simply not relevant to the structure you care about. Think of a video: the precise texture of the grass, the exact position of each leaf moving in the wind, the noise of the sensor. These are high-entropy degrees of freedom, and a model that predicts in pixel space must spend its capacity, and its data, learning to reproduce them. That's wasteful, and in some sense it's hopeless, because much of it is unpredictable in principle.

From the point of view of someone coming from physics, the appealing thing about predicting in a latent space is that it resembles coarse-graining. You throw away the microscopic details and you retain the variables that have some predictive power at larger scales, in space or in time. And the key empirical fact about natural data, which I think we don't yet fully understand theoretically, is that it is organized hierarchically and compositionally. There are low-level features that combine into intermediate ones, which combine into objects, scenes, and so on. If the representation you predict is at the right level of that hierarchy, then the prediction problem becomes much more constrained, and you need fewer samples to learn it.

We have some theoretical understanding of this in simplified models. If you take a generative process with a hierarchical, tree-like structure, you can show that the sample complexity for learning the task depends on how deep in the hierarchy you need to go to see the correlations that matter. Learning at the pixel level means you must discover those correlations starting from the bottom, and the number of samples required to resolve the relevant statistics at each level can be large. If instead the model builds and predicts representations that are already somewhat abstract, you're effectively learning from data with much smaller effective dimension, and the curse of dimensionality is less severe.

Now I want to be careful, because there's a circularity here: the latent representation has to be learned, and it has to be learned without collapsing to something trivial. That's where a lot of the engineering difficulty lies, and I don't think the theory is mature. But the principle, that you should predict what is predictable and discard what is noise, seems to me the right one. It's in the end a statement about where the information in the data lives, and the pixel space is almost certainly the wrong place to look for it.

astra-6.text:
Well, if you predict pixels, you are asking the system to predict an enormous amount of detail that may be irrelevant to what you want to learn. If I show you a scene with a tree, the exact positions of all the leaves are very difficult to predict, but you may not need them to understand what is happening. So the concern is that a lot of data and model capacity go into describing those details.

Predicting a latent representation gives you the possibility of selecting the information that matters. You can try to predict something about the objects, their relationships, or how they evolve, without specifying every pixel. If that representation captures the underlying structure, then many observations that look different become examples of the same thing. That is where you could gain sample efficiency.

For tokens, the distinction is less sharp, because language is already quite abstract. But predicting the exact next token still asks you to model choices of wording that may not matter for the underlying meaning.

Of course, the difficult part is learning the representation. You cannot simply throw information away: you must keep what is useful, and avoid a trivial representation that predicts itself perfectly because it contains nothing. So I see this as a promising route, rather than a guarantee. The potential advantage comes from learning what to predict, as well as learning how to predict it.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you predict pixels, you’re asking the system to predict a lot of things that may not matter for understanding the world. Think of a video: the exact texture of a surface, the lighting, all these details can be difficult to predict, even when the underlying event is quite simple. Predicting tokens is more abstract already, but you’re still rewarded for predicting the particular token that occurs.

The hope with latent representations is that you can learn a space in which the relevant structure is retained and some of that variability is discarded. Then predicting what happens next could become a much simpler problem. If many different observations correspond to the same underlying situation, you can share what you learn across them, rather than having to learn each variation separately. That’s where you might gain sample efficiency.

But the important qualification is that the representation has to retain useful information. A constant representation is perfectly predictable and completely useless. So the question is really how to learn representations that simplify prediction without throwing away the structure you need. That’s the promise, but also the central difficulty.
